title: Montesquieu's Other Warning: The Tyranny of Opinion
hook: Montesquieu is famous for separation of powers. His lesser-known warning: a constitution can be free on paper and still fail, once enough people stop believing its limits apply to them.
key_points: Montesquieu's The Spirit of the Laws (1748) shaped the Founders' separation of powers — at the Constitutional Convention, only the Bible was cited more.
He defined political liberty not as 'doing what one wants,' but as the security of being governed by known, stable laws rather than arbitrary power.
His deeper warning: even a well-designed constitution fails when people's moral convictions clash with what the law allows — then 'the Constitution will be free by right and not in fact.'
When a law stops people from doing what they feel morally bound to do, they experience it as oppression, whatever its constitutional legitimacy.
The idea helps explain why deep polarization is corrosive: opposing sides can each see the other's lawful governance as illegitimate.
content_html: Everyone learns the Montesquieu of separation of powers: split government into branches so no one part can dominate the others. James Madison called him "the oracle who is always consulted and cited" on that point, and at the Constitutional Convention only the Bible was quoted more often than his Spirit of the Laws (1748).
extra_html: Montesquieu had a second, less-quoted argument. He defined political liberty not as doing whatever one likes, but as "a tranquility of mind arising from the opinion each person has of his safety" — the security that comes from living under known, stable laws instead of arbitrary power. But he also warned that formal structure isn't enough on its own: a constitution can be perfectly designed and still fail in practice if people's cultural or moral convictions come to clash with what the law permits. As Robert A. Ballingall, a political scientist at the University of Maine, writes in The Conversation, Montesquieu's phrase for that failure is that the constitution becomes "free by right and not in fact" — legally intact, but no longer accepted as legitimate by people who feel the law is blocking what they believe they're owed. Applied to today, the argument is symmetric rather than partisan: when opposing groups hold incompatible convictions — on immigration, gender, religion, or anything else — each can experience the other side's lawful governance as illegitimate oppression, regardless of what the Constitution's text actually says. That, more than any single law, is what corrodes a constitutional order from within. (This card describes a general theory of constitutional legitimacy, illustrated with U.S. examples; the underlying dynamic applies across constitutional democracies.)

authors: Robert A. Ballingall, Associate Professor of Political Science, University of Maine

related.title: Key Political Thinkers
related.hook: A handful of thinkers, writing across two millennia, still frame the questions we argue about: who should rule, why obey, and how to stop power going bad?

related.title: Separation of Powers
related.hook: Split government into branches that make, enforce, and interpret the law — so no single part can do all three.

related.title: Political Legitimacy
related.hook: Power can rest on fear alone, but it lasts when people believe it is rightful. That belief — legitimacy — is what separates authority from mere force.

flashcards.prompt: Besides separation of powers, what did Montesquieu warn could undo even a well-designed constitution?
flashcards.back_html: A gap between the law and people's moral convictions. When citizens feel entitled to ignore constitutional limits, the constitution is "free by right and not in fact."

flashcards.prompt: How did Montesquieu define political liberty?

choices.text: Security from arbitrary power, from being governed by stable, known laws
Doing whatever one wants without restraint
A freedom that only rulers can exercise

flashcards.explanation_html: He rejected the idea that liberty means unrestrained action — true freedom, for him, comes from laws that remove the fear of arbitrary government or arbitrary neighbors.

flashcards.prompt: Per the 'tyranny of opinion' idea, why can deep polarization threaten a constitutional order?

choices.text: Each side may see the other's lawful governance as illegitimate, eroding the shared belief the system depends on
Polarization is itself illegal under most constitutions
It always leads directly to a change in government

flashcards.explanation_html: Montesquieu's warning is about legitimacy, not legality: a constitution can be lawful on paper while its authority is no longer accepted in practice.
